props.title: Fires Were Started

sections.content: Humphrey Jennings' **Fires Were Started (1943)** (1943) stands as one of the most influential British documentary films ever made, revolutionizing the docudrama format during WWII. Unlike pure propaganda pieces like London Can Take It! (1940), Jennings used real firefighters to recreate their experiences battling blazes during the Blitz. This groundbreaking approach influenced later war documentaries like **The Battle of San Pietro** (1945) and established a template for mixing authentic subjects with dramatic reconstruction that echoes through works like **The Battle of Algiers** (1966).

sections.content: The film's impact on British documentary tradition cannot be overstated. Its influence runs through the Free Cinema movement of the 1950s, particularly visible in **Every Day Except Christmas** (1957) and **We Are the Lambeth Boys** (1959). Jennings' careful balance of realism and artistry created a distinctly British documentary aesthetic that influenced filmmakers from Lindsay Anderson to Ken Loach, whose **Cathy Come Home** (1966) follows similar docudrama techniques.

The film's innovative use of real firefighters performing reconstructed scenes created a new form of authenticity in documentary filmmaking. This approach influenced later works like **The War Game** (1965) and **Culloden** (1964) by Peter Watkins, who pushed the docudrama format into more experimental territory. The tension between documentary truth and dramatic reconstruction that Jennings explored continues to resonate in contemporary films like **United 93** (2006). sections.content: Post-war documentary filmmakers built directly on Jennings' innovations. The observational style of **Housing Problems** (1935) combined with Jennings' dramatic approach created a new pathway for social documentary. This influence is particularly visible in the work of the National Film Board of Canada, especially in films like **Lonely Boy** (1962) and continues through to modern hybrid documentaries like **The Act of Killing** (2012).
